newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Aid sex slaves to catch traffickers, Euro-MP urges.
newsitem.headline: Aid sex slaves to catch traffickers, Euro-MP urges.

text.p: Women smuggled into the European Union to work as prostitutes should be granted temporary residence permits by EU governments if they are prepared to give evidence in court, a Euro-MP said on Friday.

"There's no way these traffickers can be caught if the witnesses do not come forward, and we can't get them to stand up in court if they can't get protection," British Labour Euro-MP Sue Waddington told Reuters.
Waddington is the author of a report on sexual exploitation which she hopes the European Parliament will adopt in September.
Victims needed emergency phone lines, safe houses and temporary resident status pending a decision on whether they should be allowed to remain permanently in the EU, she said.

They also needed legal aid, translators, advice on asylum rights and, while in the EU, an income which would help them get out of the poverty trap that led them to buy the traffickers' false promise of a golden future in the first place.

EU governments had already committed themselves to temporary residence and income support for victims of sexual exploitation, Waddington said, but she wanted the European Commission to check if they were fulfilling these pledges and report back next year.

Waddington said sexual exploitation -- which the EU says ensnares half a million women every year -- could only be fought effectively if the problem was tackled from all angles and this meant fighting both its causes and its consequences.

A growing number of women were being smuggled in from the central and east European countries seeking EU membership so Union aid to help these states catch up with the bloc's existing 15 members should be targeted more closely at improving the economic, social and legal status of their female population.

More EU money should be made available to non-governmental organisations running campaigns to warn women in Eastern Europe and the developing world about the dangers of "recruitment agencies" offering them fictitious jobs in the gold-paved West rich as dancers, waiters or au pairs.
The NGOs also needed more money to aid victims, who were more likely to trust them than the authorities, Waddington said.
The EU has set aside a modest 10 million ecus ($10.8 million) to aid sex slaves between now and the year 2000 but NGOs have found it difficult to access the funds, the Waddington said.
